title: National Airspace System
summary: Read the airspace around your route, then connect its boundaries to entry, equipment, weather, and pilot requirements.
objectives: Identify the class and boundaries of airspace using current charts and airport information.
Distinguish an explicit clearance, established communications, equipment rules, and weather minimums.
Explain how special-use airspace, TFRs, and pilot-specific restrictions change a route decision.

sections.title: Read airspace in three dimensions
sections.body:
A chart is a plan view of a three-dimensional structure. To identify your airspace, determine the lateral boundary, floor, ceiling, and time of operation. Then compare your altitude with the correct reference: MSL is measured from mean sea level, while AGL is measured above the surface beneath you.

Class B shelves use solid blue boundaries and charted MSL floors and ceilings. Class C uses solid magenta, Class D uses dashed blue, and a Class E surface area uses dashed magenta. A magenta vignette commonly marks a 700 ft AGL Class E floor; a blue vignette marks a 1,200 ft AGL floor. Read the chart legend and special annotations rather than treating color alone as a complete rule.

Apply it: flying underneath a Class B shelf does not put you inside the shelf. It also does not automatically remove an overlapping transponder, ADS-B, speed, or nearby surface-airspace requirement.
sections.deep:
MSL shelves remain referenced to sea level while the ground rises beneath them, so their height above terrain changes. A 700 ft AGL transition floor follows terrain conceptually rather than describing a constant MSL shelf. The two references answer different questions.

Class G is the uncontrolled airspace left outside controlled airspace; it does not have one universal nationwide top. Class E can begin at the surface, 700 ft AGL, 1,200 ft AGL, or another designated altitude. Tower closure can change an airport’s surface-airspace classification, but a surrounding transition area does not necessarily disappear. Use the Chart Supplement’s actual operating-hours and airspace notes.

sections.title: Entry rules: clearance is different from contact
sections.body:
ClassUsual entry principle
ANormally IFR operation with the required clearance, pilot qualifications, and equipment; generally 18,000 ft MSL through FL600.
BReceive an explicit ATC clearance before entry; satisfy pilot and equipment requirements.
C or DEstablish two-way communications with the responsible ATC facility before entry and maintain them.
E or GNo general airspace-entry radio requirement for ordinary VFR; other airport, equipment, and operating rules can apply.

In Class C or D, a response containing your aircraft identification establishes communications unless ATC instructs you to remain outside. A response to “aircraft calling” does not identify you. In Class B, even a callsign response or flight-following service does not replace the explicit entry clearance.
sections.deep:
Ask four separate questions: Is this pilot qualified? Is the aircraft equipped? Has the required communication or clearance occurred? Are the weather and other operating conditions legal? A yes to one does not supply the others.

Student, sport, and recreational privileges have additional limitations and endorsements. Some Class B primary airports have stricter pilot-certificate restrictions. An operating control tower in Class E or G can impose communications requirements near the airport even though the airspace class has no blanket entry call requirement. Teach the local example with the applicable regulation and Chart Supplement open, instead of memorizing “E means no radio” as an absolute.

sections.title: Visibility and clouds: identify the row before the mnemonic
sections.body:
Basic VFR weather minimums depend on class, altitude, and sometimes height above the surface and time of day. These are airplane training summaries; § 91.155 contains the complete rule and exceptions.

SituationFlight visibilityCloud separation
Class B3 SMClear of clouds
Class C/D; Class E below 10,000 ft MSL3 SM500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontally
E at or above 10,000 ft MSL5 SM1,000 ft below and above, 1 SM horizontally
G, at or below 1,200 ft AGL, day1 SMClear of clouds
G, at or below 1,200 ft AGL, night3 SM500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontally
sections.deep:
In Class G more than 1,200 ft above the surface but below 10,000 ft MSL, the usual airplane minimum is 1 SM by day or 3 SM at night, with the 500/1,000/2,000 ft cloud distances. Above 1,200 ft AGL and at or above 10,000 ft MSL, it becomes 5 SM with 1,000 ft above/below and 1 SM horizontal separation. Section 91.155 includes limited exceptions, including certain airport-pattern operations.

The reason for space around clouds is traffic that can emerge from them, including aircraft operating legally under IFR. Under § 91.155(c), basic VFR beneath a ceiling within controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport generally requires a ceiling of at least 1,000 ft; the special-VFR exception has separate conditions. Pilot-specific limits may be more restrictive: a student pilot must apply § 61.89 visibility and surface-reference requirements in addition to the airspace table.

sections.title: Equipment overlays can extend outside the class boundary
sections.body:
Transponder and ADS-B Out requirements overlap with airspace classes but do not match them perfectly. For ordinary electrically equipped airplanes, significant ADS-B Out areas include Class B and C, the specified 30 NM Class B airport veil, airspace above Class B/C within their lateral boundaries up to 10,000 ft MSL, and applicable high-altitude Class E. Section 91.225 also contains the coastal Gulf requirement, exceptions, and deviation procedures.

At and above 10,000 ft MSL in the contiguous states and DC, the Class E ADS-B requirement excludes airspace at or below 2,500 ft above the surface. Apply the actual rule rather than an unqualified “above ten thousand” slogan. Transponder requirements are separately defined in § 91.215.

Common trap: ADS-B In on a tablet is a receiver. It does not satisfy an ADS-B Out transmission requirement and does not show every aircraft.
sections.deep:
ADS-B is automatic because the equipment broadcasts without a radar interrogation. It is dependent because the report depends on onboard navigation and other aircraft data. A GNSS-derived position is not the same as worldwide delivery of the report: the normal terrestrial radio link and ground reception still have coverage and line-of-sight limits.

TIS-B and ADS-R can supplement traffic awareness; FIS-B supplies certain flight information to compatible receivers. Service availability depends on equipment, coverage, and the service involved. A blank traffic display does not establish an empty sky. The see-and-avoid responsibility remains, and datalink weather latency makes it unsuitable for close-range thunderstorm penetration decisions.

sections.title: Speed and separation depend on the operation
sections.body:
For ordinary domestic operations, § 91.117 generally limits indicated airspeed below 10,000 ft MSL to 250 kt. At or below 2,500 ft above the surface within 4 NM of a Class C or D primary airport, the usual limit is 200 kt. Beneath a Class B area or in a designated VFR corridor through it, the limit is 200 kt. Read the full rule for the specific authorizations and minimum-safe-airspeed exception.

These limits use indicated airspeed, not groundspeed. An ordinary heading, route, or flight-following instruction does not mean the pilot may ignore an applicable speed limit.

Controlled airspace also does not mean every VFR aircraft receives the same separation service. Class B separates participating aircraft; Class C includes VFR/IFR separation. Ordinary Class D service does not supply general VFR separation. Continue the appropriate visual scan.
sections.deep:
Traffic sequencing, traffic information, and separation are related but different services. Being placed behind another airplane in a landing sequence does not remove the pilot’s collision-avoidance responsibilities. Know what the facility is actually providing and clarify instructions when the traffic picture is uncertain.

Speed affects the time available to see, decide, and maneuver near a conflict. The same geographic distance disappears faster with a higher closure rate, even though your own indicated speed may appear moderate. Teach students to manage speed and workload early, use radio information to focus their scan, and avoid turning a traffic display into their only source of awareness.

sections.title: Special VFR is a limited clearance, not a weather escape plan
sections.body:
Special VFR allows qualifying operations below basic VFR minimums in certain airport surface areas, with an ATC clearance. For airplanes, the basic special-VFR conditions include remaining clear of clouds and at least 1 SM flight visibility. Takeoff and landing also require at least 1 SM ground visibility when reported, or the specified flight-visibility condition when it is not.

It applies within the lateral boundaries of eligible Class B, C, D, or E airport surface areas below 10,000 ft MSL. It does not create a route-wide exemption or authorize an ordinary Class E surface-area extension. Some airports prohibit fixed-wing special VFR.

Between sunset and sunrise, the airplane pilot must meet the applicable instrument-flight requirements and the aircraft must have the required IFR equipment. Pilot-specific privileges and limitations still apply. A special-VFR clearance never guarantees obstacle clearance or safe conditions beyond its limits.
sections.deep:
The clearance solves a traffic-separation problem inside a defined area; it does not solve terrain visibility, deteriorating weather, pilot proficiency, or the transition into surrounding airspace. Before considering it, ask what weather exists along the entire intended route and what legal, safe conditions will exist after leaving the surface area.

For a student, do not substitute the 1 SM special-VFR minimum for § 61.89’s higher visibility limits or required visual reference to the surface. Instructor restrictions and endorsements still matter. A CFI should teach the full eligibility analysis rather than treating special VFR as an automatic right, a minimum-weather target, or a universal student-pilot workaround.

sections.title: Special-use airspace and temporary restrictions
sections.body:
Restricted and prohibited areas are regulatory. Their legal descriptions and controlling or using agencies matter. Restricted-area activity, scheduling, and authorization determine whether entry is permitted. A prohibited area requires specific authorization; never assume ordinary flight following clears it.

MOAs separate military activity from certain other operations. VFR entry is generally possible without a clearance, but high-speed military traffic makes activity status and a conservative routing decision important. Alert and warning areas communicate hazards. Controlled firing areas use monitoring and suspension of activity to protect nonparticipating aircraft, so they are not normally charted like an MOA.

Apply it: review current charts, NOTAMs, and authoritative TFR information before flight and update when conditions change. An EFB’s shaded shape can lag or omit details; the actual notice defines location, times, altitudes, exceptions, and contacts.
sections.deep:
Do not confuse permission with prudence. An inactive restricted area may be available subject to its published provisions, while a legally accessible active MOA can still be an unsuitable place for a basic lesson. Ask the controlling agency for status when appropriate and retain a route that remains acceptable if access is unavailable.

Publication currency is also a layered problem. A current sectional does not include every temporary change, and a current database does not guarantee current receiver software or valid operating approval. Check each product’s effective dates and applicable NOTAMs rather than assuming every publication shares one update cycle. Use chart symbols as an index to the controlling information.

teachBack: On a current local sectional, identify one route point’s class, altitude reference, entry requirement, weather minimums, and equipment overlays.
Explain why hearing your callsign is sufficient for one type of airspace entry but not for another.
Explain what information a TFR notice supplies that a colored EFB outline cannot establish.
takeaways: Determine exact boundaries and operating times before applying a rule.
Clearance, communications, pilot privileges, equipment, and weather are separate checks.
Legally accessible airspace can still be a poor operational choice.

quiz.question: Approach replies, “Cessna 12345, standby,” before your planned Class C entry and gives no instruction to remain outside. What has occurred?
options: An explicit Class B clearance has also been issued
Two-way communications have been established for Class C entry
Your equipment requirements have been waived
A landing clearance has been issued
feedback: Class B requires an explicit entry clearance; a callsign response does not supply it.
ATC used your aircraft identification, which establishes two-way communications for the Class C entry rule.
A radio response does not waive transponder or ADS-B requirements.
Landing clearance is a separate tower authorization.
quiz.hint: Identify what the controller acknowledged, and which class you are entering.

quiz.question: You remain below a Class B shelf, but are within the applicable 30 NM veil in an ordinary electrically equipped airplane. Which statement is sound?
options: The shelf floor removes every equipment requirement
ADS-B In on a tablet satisfies ADS-B Out rules
Evaluate the veil’s transponder and ADS-B Out rules separately from the shelf
Flight following automatically waives the veil requirements
feedback: The veil is an equipment overlay with boundaries different from the shelf.
A receiver does not provide the required outward broadcasts.
Being outside the Class B volume does not alone remove the separate equipment overlay.
Routine traffic advisory service is not an equipment deviation authorization.
quiz.hint: Separate the three-dimensional class boundary from an equipment overlay.

quiz.question: An airplane is in Class E below 10,000 ft MSL under ordinary basic VFR. Which set gives the usual minimum flight visibility and cloud separation?
options: 1 SM and clear of clouds
3 SM and clear of clouds
5 SM, 1,000 ft above/below, and 1 SM horizontal
3 SM, 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, and 2,000 ft horizontal
feedback: That set resembles low-level Class G daytime conditions, not ordinary Class E.
Clear of clouds with 3 SM is the Class B set.
That is the Class E set at or above 10,000 ft MSL.
This is the ordinary Class E minimum below 10,000 ft MSL.
quiz.hint: Choose the correct altitude row before recalling the cloud distances.

quiz.question: A magenta vignette on a sectional normally depicts which Class E transition floor?
options: 700 ft AGL
1,200 ft AGL
700 ft MSL
14,500 ft MSL
feedback: The magenta vignette commonly marks the 700 ft above-ground transition floor.
A blue vignette marks a 1,200 ft AGL transition floor.
The vignette’s reference is above ground level rather than sea level.
The vignette is not a generic 14,500 ft MSL boundary.
quiz.hint: Pay attention to both the color and the altitude reference.

quiz.question: A special-VFR airplane departs an eligible airport surface area. What must the pilot evaluate when leaving that area?
options: The clearance removes cloud limits for the entire trip
Legal and safe conditions for the surrounding airspace and remaining route
ATC will provide terrain clearance throughout the route
The minimum visibility becomes the Class B value everywhere
feedback: The clearance is limited to eligible surface airspace and still requires cloud clearance.
Special VFR does not create a route-wide exemption or guarantee conditions outside the area.
Terrain and obstacle responsibility remains with the pilot.
Weather requirements depend on the actual airspace and operating circumstances.
quiz.hint: Consider where the special clearance’s geographic authority ends.

quiz.question: Your EFB shows no traffic while you cross an active MOA under VFR. What is the best conclusion?
options: There cannot be military aircraft nearby
ATC has automatically separated your flight from every military aircraft
The display may omit traffic; confirm activity and consider a safer route
VFR entry into every MOA is automatically illegal
feedback: Traffic displays can omit aircraft or lack complete service coverage.
VFR traffic advisory services do not guarantee separation from all military activity.
Incomplete traffic information and potentially high-speed activity justify checking status and reassessing the route.
MOAs generally do not require a VFR entry clearance, but legal access does not eliminate the hazard.
quiz.hint: Distinguish a surveillance display’s coverage from the actual traffic environment.
